phonemes.desc: Short alpha with smooth breathing, unstressed opening.
Aspirated kappa with acute on short epsilon [kʰé], the pitch peak.
Rho-omega-nu, a long second syllable giving the name its weight and length.

pronunciation.approximation: 'ah-KHAY-rohn' — the middle syllable is pitched high; the final -ōn is long and sonorous.

kin.label: Greek
kin.form: Ἀχέρων (Achérōn), the river of woe in the underworld

kin.label: Etymology
kin.form: Possibly from ἄχος (áchos), 'grief, pain'; etymology uncertain

kin.label: Geography
kin.form: A real river in Thesprotia, Epirus, identified with the underworld river

pronunciation.note: Achérōn is Tier 1 because the Greek Ἀχέρων contains both stress (acute on έ) and length (ω). The name is at once a real river in Epirus and the mythic boundary of Hades.

domains.title: River of Woe
domains.subtitle: Underworld Boundary, Grief, Passage
domains.lead: Achérōn is the river of woe, one of the great boundary rivers of the Greek underworld. Real in Epirus and mythic in Hades, it marks the place where the living must stop and the dead begin their journey.

cards.name: Boundary of Hades
cards.desc: One of the rivers that separate the world of the living from the dead.

cards.name: River of Grief
cards.desc: Its waters are identified with ἄχος, the Greek word for pain and sorrow.

cards.name: Real and Mythic
cards.desc: The Thesprotian Acheron was believed to be an entrance to the underworld.

cards.name: Ferry and Guide
cards.desc: The dead must cross its waters, sometimes by Charon's boat.

mythology.lead: Achérōn is less a character than a place of passage. Its mythology is the geography of death: where the rivers flow, who ferries the dead, and what must be left behind.

myths.title: Child of Oceanus
myths.text: Hesiod makes Acheron a son of Oceanus and Tethys, one of the great world-encircling rivers. From this genealogy comes its cosmic status: it is not merely a local stream but a branch of the primordial waters.

myths.title: Odysseus at the Acheron
myths.text: In Odyssey 10, Circe sends Odysseus to the edges of Oceanus and the Acheron to summon the dead. There he digs a trench, pours libations, and calls up the shades of Tiresias, his mother Anticleia, and the heroines of old. The river is the membrane between epic and necromancy.

myths.title: The Stygian Confluence
myths.text: Virgil places Acheron at the entrance to the underworld, where Charon ferries the souls of the dead. The river is fed by Cocytus and Phlegethon, and its murky waters mirror the grief of those who cross it.

lore.syncretism: The Greek underworld rivers were mapped onto real landscapes, especially the Thesprotian Acheron, where an oracle of the dead (Nekromanteion) operated. Roman poets Virgil and Ovid developed the river's role in the geography of Hades. Christian tradition transformed the Acheron into one of the rivers of hell, often conflated with the Styx. The name survives in modern Greek geography and in every reference to 'Acheron' as a symbol of sorrow.
lore.culturalLegacy: Achérōn is the river whose name means grief. It appears in Dante's Inferno, in Romantic poetry, and in every metaphor that turns a dark stream into the threshold of death. The real Acheron in Epirus still carries the name, its waters a tourist route to an ancient oracle of the dead. The boundary between geography and myth remains thin there.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Achérōn is the first river we cannot cross alone. In the myth, the dead need a ferry and a coin; they must leave the body behind and pay for passage. The river therefore marks not just death but transition: the moment when the old self is no longer sufficient.

Grief flows like a river because it too has no final shore. We cross and recross it, carried by memory, paying with tears. Achérōn reminds us that sorrow is a geography, not an event — a landscape with real rivers, real reeds, and real crossings. To name it in Unicode is to acknowledge that grief, like a river, has its own ancient right of way.
lore.archaeology: The Nekromanteion, an oracle of the dead, was located near the mouth of the Acheron in Thesprotia (modern Mesopotamos). Excavations revealed an underground labyrinth used for incubation and necromantic ritual. The river itself, with its springs and underground passages, reinforced the belief that this was an entrance to Hades. Roman travelers including Pliny and Pausanias noted the site.
